issues.issue: The date is left blank ("made as of June __, 2004"), so the instrument's effective date cannot be determined from its own face. That is a mechanical omission a court could be asked to fill.
The preamble identifies DMSA as a New Jersey corporation while Schedule A gives it a Pennsylvania address, a minor discrepancy between the preamble and the schedule it incorporates.
"Unless the context otherwise requires" leaves open when a defined meaning yields to context, but the phrase is standard boilerplate.

"Control" is defined as the power to direct management and policies "directly or indirectly ... by contract or otherwise," a boundary that is inherently fact-dependent. Whether a given DMSA-related entity is an "Affiliate" could be argued either way.
Section 10.1(i) requires the books to be kept with "a copy of ... the Certificate," a term never defined, while this definition uses "Articles." The mismatch is trivial but real.

The definition fixes contributions by reference to Section 4.1/Schedule A, and Schedule A records LSB's contribution as the garbled figure "$00,001.00," so the "aggregate amount of money" contributed is not ascertainable. The conflict is with Schedule A as incorporated by Section 4.1(i).

"Covered Person" sweeps in a long chain of persons ending in "any employee or agent of the Company or its Affiliates," and it is not clear whether the Affiliates of a Member's officers are inside or outside the list. The reach of the enumeration is arguable.
Section 17.11 confers rights under the Agreement on no Person "except the Members and Managers," yet this definition underpins the indemnification right in Section 12.4 for a much wider class.

The definition is garbled — "such Member's interest of the profits and losses" and "represents any Member Votes held by a member" — leaving unclear whether an Interest is a unitary bundle or severable economic and voting components. That matters for the transfer provisions.

Clause (iii) makes all "policies, practices and guidelines of any governmental body" a "Law," a general sweep sitting oddly against the specific legal instruments enumerated in (i) and (ii). Its outer reach is uncertain.

"Majority" is defined as "a majority of the Member Votes" while "Majority Vote" means approval by Members holding a majority of Votes; the two near-identical terms are used interchangeably for quorum and for decision. A reader could confuse the presence requirement with the voting requirement.

"Members" is defined as "two (2) or more of such Persons," so the plural term has no referent if only one member remains, yet the Agreement uses "Members" throughout for consent requirements. The definition is capable of an unintended reading.

Member Votes are fixed by Schedule A "as may be amended," while Section 2.1(iii) lets the Secretary update Schedule A and declares such updates not to be amendments — which sits uneasily with Section 17.10's requirement of unanimity for amendments. Voting power could be altered without unanimous consent.

"[A]ny amounts determined by the Members to be necessary to provide a reasonable reserve for working-capital needs or any other contingencies" gives an unbounded discretionary deduction with no standard for "reasonable" or "other contingencies." The size of Net Cash Flow can be argued either way.
The deduction is committed to "the Members," while Section 9.2 commits the timing and amount of all distributions to the Board; the two decision-makers are not reconciled.

The definition simultaneously fixes Percentage Interest "as shown on Schedule A" and "as determined by the unanimous written consent of the Members as adjusted from time to time," leaving unclear which governs if the two diverge.

Section 2.1(iii) empowers the Secretary unilaterally to update Schedule A and says such revisions are not amendments, which cannot be squared with this definition's requirement of unanimous written consent to adjust Percentage Interests.

The definition of "Person" lists "any individual, Company, association ..." using the capitalised defined term "Company," which means Dialogo, LLC itself — an evident mis-capitalisation for "corporation."

Profits and Losses are defined as taxable income under § 703(a), while Section 15.3 distributes on Capital Account balances maintained under Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iv), which requires book rather than tax figures. The two measures are not harmonised.

This clause lets the Secretary update Schedule A and declares such updates not to be amendments, while Schedule A fixes Percentage Interests and Member Votes that the "Percentage Interest" definition and Section 17.10 make alterable only by unanimous consent. The two cannot both stand.

Gerry Pike is directed to file the Articles although he is not a party or a defined role, whereas Section 2.6 assigns comparable filing duties to the Secretary. The allocation of authorised-person duties is inconsistent.

The power to change the registered agent is given to "the Members," while Section 2.6 and Section 2.5 give comparable qualification and location powers to the Board; the Agreement does not say by what vote the Members act here.

The purpose clause states a specific object — "developing Spanish language newspaper(s) and media" — and then a wholly general one, "any lawful act or activity for which limited liability companies may be formed," leaving the scope of "the business" of the Company uncertain. That scope is what fixes the reach of LSB's exclusivity covenant.

Section 12.7 bars LSB from services "to the extent it relates to the business" without defining that phrase, so its content must be drawn from this open-ended purpose clause. The two provisions together leave the covenant's boundary indeterminate.

The broad enumerated powers (e.g. to borrow, to contract, to dispose of assets) are expressed without qualification, while Section 6.8 forbids any of those acts without unanimous Board approval. The relationship between the grant and the restriction is left implicit.

The contributions are fixed by Schedule A, which records LSB's contribution as "$00,001.00" against a 49% Percentage Interest and DMSA's as $50,000 against 51%; the figure is unintelligible and cannot be reconciled with the stated interests.

This section requires any return of Capital Contributions to be made to all Members pro rata to Percentage Interests, while Section 6.8(iii) contemplates distributions "to reimburse DMSA for initial capital contributions" alone. The two cannot both be given effect.

"[T]he respective invoices of each of DMSA" is garbled — the plural "each of" has no list — so it is unclear whose invoices the Company must pay and on what terms. The exception to the no-compensation rule is therefore indeterminate.

The clause promises Members "profits in accordance with their respective Membership Interests," a term used nowhere else (the defined term is "Percentage Interest"), and it makes profit payment mandatory while Section 9.2 leaves all distributions to the Board's discretion.

"[T]he Members shall be able only to make their capital contributions pursuant to Section 4.1" reads as a prohibition on further contributions, contradicting the second sentence of Section 4.1(ii) permitting additional contributions with unanimous written consent. The wording appears to be a drafting slip.

Section 4.1(ii) expressly permits additional capital contributions with the written consent of all Members, which this clause's "able only to make their capital contributions pursuant to Section 4.1" appears to forbid.
